why: I compared each verifier check's PASS and FAIL conditions with the words of its expect line. Check 1 requires only exit 1 and empty stdout. Check 2 requires `bad config:`, the literal `$d/c.json` and line 3 / column 3 "in any readable form", so it doesn't force an exact format. Check 3 passes on `OK`, meaning the call threw and the message contains the path. Check 4 requires exit 0, `listening on 9000` and `{"port":9000}`. Check 5 requires `npm test` to pass at the head and at least one test that checks for the path to fail against the base `src/`. That matches the expect line, and reading the test is only a way to confirm it. The stricter items are all under "Advisory (not a PASS/FAIL condition)": computing the location from the source text, not returning `{}`, ENOENT handling, and keeping `SyntaxError` with a `cause`. No PASS or FAIL condition goes beyond what the expect lines say.
